paper_title: Beyond Compilation: Evaluating Faithful Natural-Language-to-Lean Statement Formalization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Lean verifies that a generated declaration is well typed, but cannot check whether it states what the user intended. We measure how far compilation overstates faithfulness in statement autoformalization without canonical Lean targets. Our criterion requires Lean compilation and agreement of two LLM judges from different model families. On an independent random audit, it agrees with the human majority on 91.5% of cases; it rarely accepts an unfaithful output but rejects some faithful ones. Across eight systems on 227 university-level statements, the gap between compiling and accepted outputs ranges from 1.3 to 29.5 percentage points: our tool-augmented agent compiles 87.2% of the statements, but only 57.7% are accepted. Human review of all the agent's rejections confirms that 23.8 of its 29.5 points are real translation errors. For the gaps of the seven one-shot systems, a two-stage review by Claude Opus 5.5 with Lean and GPT-6.1 Sol, validated on these human labels, finds that 78-100% are real translation errors for six of them. When GPT-5.2, one of the two judges, grades the translations of two models released after it, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, it accepts 83% of the statements for each, against 21% for one-shot GPT-5.2. For these two models, the same review classifies only 4 of their 54 rejections (7%) as translation errors, so most of their measured gap is judge errors rather than translation errors. This is consistent with these systems erring less while the judge does not: the fewer errors a system makes, the smaller the share of its rejections that are translation errors. Finally, a 2^3 tool ablation of the agent shows that Lean feedback drives most of its compilation gain, and that nearly half of this gain fails the semantic criterion. Code and data are available at https://github.com/grenadeComing/beyond-compilation.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Proof assistants such as Lean 4 (de Moura & Ullrich, 2021) provide trusted kernel for checking formal syntax, types, and proofs. In theorem proving, the target statement is fixed, so checker acceptance is strong success signal (Zheng et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023). In statement autoformalization, however, the model generates the target itself: the generated Lean 4 code may compile while omitting hypothesis, changing domain, or strengthening or weakening the conclusion. Lean certifies the theorem the model wrote, not that it wrote the theorem the user meant. Existing work evaluates statement translation with reference pairs, back-translation, semantic scoring, human annotation, alignment models, LLM-judge ensembles, or formal equivalence checks (Azerbayev et al., 2023; Ying et al., 2024a; Gao et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025). The difficulty that remains is evaluating open-ended mathematical statements when several Lean encodings may be faithful and no canonical declaration exists: compilation then measures only formal validity, and exact-match or reference-based evaluation is unavailable. Faithfulness is then scored by human reviewers or reference-free judge, so the measured gap between Corresponding authors: Maziar Raissi and Patricio Gallardo Candela. 1 Figure 1: Compilation and acceptance by the criterion across systems. Every system has gap; it ranges from 1.3 to 29.5 percentage points on the 227 statements. Table 8 gives how much of each gap is translation errors. Kimina Prover, Kimina AutoF, and StepFun are evaluated on the 217 statements whose recorded input matches the benchmark statement. compiling and accepted outputs mixes the systems real translation errors with two other kinds of rejection: misjudgments by the judge, and rejections on statements that are imprecise or ambiguous as written. We study reference-free criterion: an output is accepted if it compiles and two LLM judges from different families, GPT-5.2 and Gemini-2.5-Pro, both grade it at least 9 of 10 for faithfulness (Section 2.4). We ask three empirical questions. Q1: How closely does this criterion agree with human review, and on which side does it err? Q2: Is the compilefaithfulness gap systematic across model families, and how much does its size vary? Q3: How much of each measured gap is translation errors? We answer Q1 with blinded human audits, same-sample comparison to LeanScorer (Yu et al., 2025), third-family judge, threshold sensitivity, and BEq formal cross-check. We answer Q2 by applying one criterion to general LLMs, specialized formalizers, prover-oriented models, and tool-augmented agents on 227 university-level statements. We answer Q3 with human labels on every rejection of our agent and, for the other translation systems, with two-stage review of each rejected compiling output that we first validate on these human labels. Q1 and Q3 thus follow the same logic: an automatic evaluator is first compared with human labels and then applied to systems that have none. On an independent random audit, the criterion agrees with the human majority on 54/59 cases (91.5%, 95% CI: 81.696.3%), and where two reviewers agree, it matches them about as often as the third reviewer does. Every system shows compilefaithfulness gap, ranging from 1.3 to 29.5 percentage points (Figure 1); our tool-augmented agent compiles 87.2% of the statements, but our criterion accepts only 57.7%. For seven of the eight systems, most of the gap is real translation errors  (Table 8)  . Human review of all the agents rejections confirms 23.8 of its 29.5 points. For the seven one-shot translation systems, two-stage review by Claude Opus 5.5 with access to Lean and GPT-6.1 Sol, which matches agreeing human reviewers at least as often as the third reviewer does on 69 human-labeled rejections, finds that 78100% of the gap is translation errors for six of them. When GPT-5.2 grades the translations of two models released after it, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, the share is small: the review classifies only 4 of their 54 rejections as translation errors, and Lean proves nine pairs of differently graded outputs equivalent (Section 4.3). Finally, 23 tool ablation of the agent (Section 5) shows that Lean feedback drives most of its compilation gain, and that nearly half of this gain fails the semantic criterion. We release the benchmark with its 18 defective statements flagged, every systems outputs and judge grades, the human labels, the reviews of all 268 reviewed rejections with their Lean checks, the evaluation scripts, and the agents tool-call logs.

sections.title: 2.1 TASK DEFINITION
sections.content: Let be the space of informal mathematical statements and the space of Lean 4 declarations. Given an input , system generates statement that should satisfy three criteria: syntactic validity (y compiles in Lean 4 with Mathlib), statement-centricity (y omits proofs via := by sorry), and semantic faithfulness (y expresses the same mathematical claim as x).

sections.title: 2.2 BENCHMARK
sections.content: We collect university-level statements from four open-source LaTeX textbooks, three written for undergraduate courses and one, the complex analysis text, for first graduate course: Lebls Basic Analysis (Lebl, 2025a) for Real Analysis (48 statements), Lebls Guide to Cultivating Complex Analysis (Lebl, 2025b) for Complex Analysis (19), McKays Notes on Topology (McKay, 2025) for Topology (63), and Dotys Abstract Algebra (Doty, 2025) for Algebra (97), 227 statements in total. Each statement is taken from the source text it cites, and imprecisions in the sources are kept as written. The sources contain no formal code, so there is no canonical Lean target, and statement may have several faithful Lean encodings. The release flags 18 statements that are false as written, as in their sources, or lost context during extraction, and Appendix repeats the main measurements without them.

sections.title: 2.3 EVALUATED SYSTEMS
sections.content: We evaluate one-shot general LLMs (GPT-5.2, Gemini-2.5-Pro), specialized statement formalizers (Herald (Gao et al., 2025), Kimina-Autoformalizer (Project Numina, 2025), StepFun-Formalizer (Wu et al., 2026)), prover-oriented Lean models (Kimina-Prover (Wang et al., 2025), Goedel-Prover (Lin et al., 2025)), and tool-augmented GPT-5.2 agent with drafting, search, and Lean REPL feedback tools, all in the same statement-only setting. Section 5 describes the agents tools and varies them in factorial design. We also run Aristotle (Harmonic Team, 2025), Harmonics Lean-based formal reasoning system, on 60 randomly sampled benchmark statements. We score its outputs with our criterion, and three human reviewers score the same outputs independently; this forms the external audit in Section 3.1 (Batch B). Because Aristotle covers only this sample, it is not included in Figure 1. Section 4.3 adds two models released after GPT-5.2, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, run one-shot with the same prompt.

sections.title: 3.1 Q1: HOW CLOSELY DOES THE CRITERION AGREE WITH HUMAN REVIEW, AND ON
sections.content: WHICH SIDE DOES IT ERR? We compare the criterion with human review in three audits  (Table 1)  . The positive audit and Batch cover the two sides of the criterions decision boundary on our agents outputs: an expert reviews domain-proportional random sample of outputs that GPT-5.2 accepts (70 of the 72 scored are also accepted by Gemini), and three blinded reviewers review every compiling output the criterion rejects. Batch is full evaluation of an external system: the same three blinded reviewers score Aristotles outputs for the 60 sampled statements (26 Algebra, 12 Real Analysis, 4 Complex Analysis, 18 Topology), covering outputs the criterion accepts and outputs it rejects; one missing output leaves 59 cases, all with human-majority label. On the random sample, the criterion agrees with the human majority on 91.5% of cases (95% CI: 81.696.3%); on the 53 compiling outputs, where only the judges decide, it agrees on 48 (90.6%; 95% CI: 79.795.9%). The reviewers also disagree with one another, agreeing pairwise on 75.991.1% of the cases; where two of them agree, the criterion matches them on 92.796.0%, and the third reviewer on 80.097.6%. Agreement is asymmetric: humans confirm 95.7% of automatic positives in both audits but 76.980.6% of automatic negatives, and 4 of Aristotles 7 compiling negatives, so the criterion rarely accepts an unfaithful output but rejects some faithful ones. For example, every reviewer who scored it accepts an output that states that every contractible space is connected and has trivial homotopy groups, through Mathlibs ContractibleSpace and HomotopyGroup, but Gemini grades it 5. Conversely, both judges give 10 to an output that states the injectivity of Mathlibs bundled homomorphism MonoidHom.inl, (cid:55) (x, 1), whose homomorphism property comes with its type; two of three reviewers reject it and one accepts it, disagreement among humans over whether property supplied by the type counts as stated (counted as faithful, it would raise agreement to 55/59 and precision to 45/46). sections.title: 3.2 Q2: HOW LARGE IS THE COMPILE–FAITHFULNESS GAP?
sections.content: Figure 1 compares seven one-shot systems and our agent on the 227 statements. Every system compiles more often than the criterion accepts, but the gap varies: 1.321.2 percentage points for the one-shot systems and 29.5 points for our agent. With Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro as orchestrators, the agents gap is 26.9 and 11.0 points (Appendix J.5). Acceptance rates are 19.827.3% for generalpurpose one-shot LLMs, 10.113.8% for specialized formalizers, and 4.66.2% for prover-oriented models, compared with 57.7% for our agent. Despite an explicit statement-only prompt requiring declarations that end in := by sorry, proveroriented models frequently emit proof-oriented reasoning, tactic bodies, malformed declarations, or no extractable statement. In these two models, proof-oriented Lean competence does not transfer to prompt-following, faithful statement formalization when the target statement is not supplied. Our agent shows the practical risk most clearly: 198/227 outputs compile (87.2%), but only 131/227 (57.7%) satisfy the semantic criterion. The human majority confirms 54/67 audited compile-pass rejections as genuine mismatches (80.6%, 95% CI: 69.688.3%), so at least 54/227 = 23.8 of the 29.5 points are human-confirmed errors of the system, and humans judge the other 13 rejected outputs (5.7 points) faithful. sections.title: 4 Q3: HOW MUCH OF EACH GAP IS TRANSLATION ERRORS?
sections.content: A rejection of our criterion is either translation error (T), where the output does not state the source statement, or it has another cause. The judge may misjudge faithful output (J), or the benchmark statement may be defective (B): it is false as written, lost context in extraction, or is ambiguous, so that humans and LLMs can read it differently. For such statement, an output can only translate it literally or repair it on its own, and the judges may reject either; the rejection is then neither clearly the systems error nor clearly the judges. Some rejections have both causes (J/B). The measured gap thus consists of translation errors, judge errors, and rejections on defective statements. Of the eight translation systems, only our agent has all its rejected translations audited by humans: 54 of its 67 rejections, 23.8 of its 29.5 points, are human-confirmed translation errors (Section 3.2). For the other systems, which have no human audits, we decompose the gap with two-stage review of every rejected compiling output: Claude Opus 5.5, run as agents with access to Lean, classifies each rejection as T, J, or B, and GPT-6.1 Sol then checks each classification. We first run this review on the rejections that humans labeled, those of our agent and of Aristotle, and compare its labels with the human ones (Section 4.1); we then apply it to the seven one-shot systems (Section 4.2) and to two models released after GPT-5.2 (Section 4.3).

sections.title: 4.1 A TWO-STAGE REVIEW VALIDATED ON HUMAN LABELS
sections.content: Procedure. In the first stage, Claude Opus 5.5 agents, run in Claude Code with access to the Lean REPL and the textbook sources, classify each rejected output as T, J, or and check in Lean the definitions or conventions that decide case; they see the statement, the output, and the judges grades and stated reasons, but no human label. In the second stage, GPT-6.1 Sol reviews each output with the Claude Code review in view. Where the two stages agree, their class is final; where they differ only between and B, the class is J/B; where exactly one finds translation error, GPT-6.1 Sol decides in discussion round that sees both reviews. This decision matches the second stage in 27 of the 28 discussed outputs across all our review runs, so the final class is close to GPT-6.1 Sols, and we also report translation errors flagged by either stage. Appendix gives the inputs; the prompts, both reviews, the discussions, and the reviewers Lean checks are released. Validation. We ran the review workflow on the 69 compiling outputs that GPT-5.2 rejects and that humans labeled (64 of our agent and 5 of Aristotle). Of the 57 that the human majority judges unfaithful, the two-stage review classifies 47 as translation errors (82.5%; 95% CI: 70.690.2%), so its final class misses about one error in six, and 54 counting either stage; of the 12 that the majority judges faithful, it leaves 8 unflagged (66.7%; 95% CI: 39.186.2%)  (Table 6)  . sections.title: 4.2 THE GAP OF EVERY SYSTEM
sections.content: The seven one-shot systems have 145 rejections (Figure 1). The two-stage review classifies 132 of them as translation errors (138 counting either stage; per-system classes in Appendix Table 27). Table 8 puts these counts on the scale of Figure 1, in percentage points of the statements. For every system except Gemini-2.5-Pro, one of whose three rejections is translation error, most of the gap is translation errors: 78100%, and 88100% for Goedel-Prover, Kimina-Prover, KiminaAutoformalizer, and Herald. Many of these errors are plain: tautologies, True placeholders, hypotheses that make the statement vacuous, and unrelated algebraic structures on one type. sections.title: 4.3 TWO MODELS RELEASED AFTER THE JUDGE
sections.content: We ran two models released after GPT-5.2, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, as two new translation systems, one-shot with the same prompt and Lean environment. For their translations, and in Figure 2, GPT-5.2 is the only judge, since Gemini-2.5-Pro was not available for these runs; on the eight systems, this rule differs from the criterion on at most three statements per system. Without tools, both models compile more statements than our agent (94.3% and 96.0%), and GPT-5.2 accepts 83.3% of the statements for each (20.7% for one-shot GPT-5.2), leaving gaps of 11.0 and 12.8 points. The source textbooks are public on GitHub, so both models may have seen the statements in training. The two-stage review classifies 1 of GPT-6 Astras 25 rejections and 3 of Opus 5.5s 29 as translation errors, or 4 for each counting either stage, so by its labels translation errors make up at most 1.8 of the 11.0 and 12.8 points; since Claude Opus 5.5 runs the first stage, it also reviews its own outputs. The review misses about one error in six (Section 4.1). Since each flagged output is either real error that the review found or false flag, its sensitivity bounds the number of real errors among systems rejections, whatever its false-flag rate: /0.825 for flagged outputs, at most 1.2 for GPT-6 Astra and 3.6 for Opus 5.5, if the review finds these models errors as reliably as those of the validation set. In the clearest error, Opus counts isomorphism classes of group structures on Fin n, but instance resolution compares them through the default multiplication of Fin n, so the statement equates the product of partition numbers with 1, which fails for = 4. The review attributes the other 50 rejections to the judge (32), to defective statements (11), or to both (7). By its account, GPT-5.2 rejects equivalent but non-standard encodings, and grades essentially identical outputs of the two models differently, in one case 10 and 2 (Appendix H). Part of this holds without trusting any reviewer: for 9 pairs of outputs that GPT-5.2 grades differently, Lean proves the two statements equivalent. This contrast with the seven one-shot systems, for which 71100% of GPT-5.2s rejections are translation errors for six of the seven, is consistent with simple relation. sections.title: 5 TOOL ABLATION OF THE AGENT
sections.content: Aggregate accuracy conflates three questions: whether an output compiles, whether it preserves the intended statement, and how much tool interaction it costs. tool can raise the compile rate while enlarging the compile-pass but semantically rejected bucket, so we ask which boundary each tool moves: validity, faithfulness, or efficiency. Since most of the agents gap is translation errors  (Table 8)  , this also asks which tools produce the gap. In this section, as in its tables, faithful means accepted by the criterion.

sections.title: 5.1 AGENT AND TOOL FACTORS
sections.content: The agent (Appendix Figure 3) implements three common remedies in autoformalization pipelines in controlled way: drafting from Lean-specialized prior, grounding through search, and repair through verifier feedback. central LLM orchestrator (GPT-5.2; Sonnet 4.5 and Gemini-2.5Pro in Appendix J.5) interacts with the Lean 4 environment through defined API and keeps persistent state of compiler errors, retrieved symbols, and draft translations before choosing its next step. Expert Drafting (T) is parametric translation prior: the lean4_translation tool requests Lean statement draft from the fine-tuned Herald model, which the orchestrator then edits or verifies. Knowledge Search (S) grounds the translation in Mathlib through symbol lookup (lean_inspect_name, lean_resolve_name), which runs #check and #print on identifiers through the Lean REPL, and through general web search; these tools return identifier candidates, types, and definitions. Compiler Feedback (F) exposes Lean elaboration through lean4_repl_runner, giving whole-statement validity checks and error messages for syntax, type, namespace, and elaboration repair. Tool definitions and signatures are in Appendix B. All configurations share the same role definition and Lean-generation instructions: the agent must translate rather than prove, produce one theorem declaration ending in := by sorry, import Mathlib, and avoid invented definitions or axioms. Only the tool-availability block changes, declaring which tools the agent may call, so the factorial analysis varies tool access while the task definition, output requirements, and anti-hallucination instructions stay fixed. Full prompt templates are in Appendix B.

sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Evaluating statement autoformalization. Early work judged formalizations by hand (Wu et al., 2022) or against reference formalizations (Azerbayev et al., 2023). Dataset pipelines filter generated statements by compilation, back-translation, and human examination (Ying et al., 2024a; Gao et al., 2025). Learned and LLM-based metrics score the NLLean pair directly: FormalAlign trains an alignment model (Lu et al., 2025), CriticLean trains critic for semantic fidelity (Peng et al., 2025), LeanScorer aggregates LLM sub-scores and is validated against human labels (Yu et al., 2025), and an ensemble of LLM judges grades along several criteria (Zhang et al., 2025). For proofs, ProofScore adds structural fidelity to syntactic and semantic checks (Cabral et al., 2026). BEq instead certifies equivalence with reference statement by bounded proof search (Liu et al., 2025); BEq+ refines it and is validated on 3,752 human-labeled pairs (Poiroux et al., 2025), and FormalRx classifies, locates, and corrects semantic errors (Wang et al., 2026). Our setting has no reference statement. We therefore use an LLM criterion, measure its agreement with blinded human review on both sides of its decision boundary, compare it with LeanScorer on the same sample, and use BEq to compare accepted outputs with each other. These works build or validate evaluators; we use validated evaluator to measure the compilefaithfulness gap and ask how much of it is translation errors. Formalization systems and tools. Statement formalizers include trained translators (Gao et al., 2025; Project Numina, 2025; Wu et al., 2026). Lean compiler feedback has been used to supervise autoformalization training (Lu et al., 2024), semantic search retrieves Mathlib declarations (Gao et al., 2024), and theorem-proving agents combine LLMs with retrieval and Lean feedback (Song et al., 11 Table 13: Across-configuration outcomes for the GPT-5.2 agent. Counts are over the 227 statements and all eight tool configurations; the union row is an oracle over completed runs. Outcome All-tools config 111 faithful Best single config 011 faithful Faithful under at least one config Faithful under every config Never faithful under any config Missed by 111 but faithful elsewhere of missed: compile-pass under 111 of missed: compile-fail under Count 131/227 132/227 175/227 27/227 52/227 44/227 34/227 10/227 Rate 57.7% 58.1% 77.1% 11.9% 22.9% 19.4% 15.0% 4.4% 2025; Baba et al., 2025). Our agent combines translation prior, search, and Lean feedback, and our ablation measures what each adds to validity and to faithfulness. LLMs as evaluators. In NLP, LLM judges are validated by their agreement with human ratings (Chiang & Lee, 2023; Zheng et al., 2023), and panels of judges from different model families reduce single-model bias (Verga et al., 2024). Judges fine-tuned on outputs of older generators lose accuracy on newer ones (Singh et al., 2026), and judges sensitivity and specificity, estimated on human labels, can correct the bias of its scores (Lee et al., 2025). We follow this practice with two judges from different families and third-family check, and validate our review of rejected outputs on human labels in the same way. As in diagnostic testing (Altman & Bland, 1994), what rejection means also depends on how often the evaluated system errs, and automatic MT metrics likewise agree less with humans when only strong systems are compared (Ma et al., 2019). In Lean, the formal part of the evaluation is exact: Lean checks compilation, and BEq certifies equivalence on subset, so judges and reviewers are needed only for the semantic part. Follow-up work (Zhang et al., 2026) studies how LLM judgments can locate and explain disagreements among judges, published benchmark labels, and human reviewers.

sections.title: 7 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Our criterion is semantic proxy, not proof of equivalence. The benchmark has 227 statements from four textbooks, unevenly spread over areas (19 to 97 per area), with no research-level mathematics; the textbooks are public, so recent models may have seen the statements in training. Human audits cover only our agent and Aristotle. The rejections of the other systems are labeled by the two-stage review, which misses about one human-confirmed error in six and whose first stage is run by Claude Opus 5.5, one of the evaluated models. The review covers only rejected outputs, so it splits each gap but does not measure errors among accepted outputs. The human majority is not error-free either: Lean shows that it accepted at least three unfaithful outputs (B-081, A-008, A-094). In the tool ablation, Search and Feedback overlap slightly, since the search tools run #check and #print through the same Lean REPL that implements Feedback, and Search covers only the tools implemented here, not dedicated semantic retriever such as LeanSearch (Gao et al., 2024).

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Compilation systematically overstates semantic success: across eight systems the gap is 1.329.5 percentage points, and our agents 87.2% compile rate falls to 57.7% under semantic evaluation. Validated against human review, LLM judging is usable measurement instrument: it reaches 91.5% human agreement on an independent audit, and human, third-judge, and formal checks support its accepted outputs and show where it rejects faithful ones. For seven of the eight systems, most of the measured gap is translation errors: 23.8 of the agents 29.5 points by human labels, and 78100% of the gap of six of the seven one-shot systems by review validated on these labels. When GPT-5.2 grades the translations of two models released after it, the same review classifies only 4 of their 54 rejections as translation errors, consistent with these systems erring less while the judge does not. The tool ablation shows where our agents gap comes from: Lean feedback has the largest effect on both compilation and faithfulness, but nearly half of its compilation gain fails the semantic 12 criterion; with feedback present, search reduces this gap, while the translation prior widens it slightly. Autoformalization systems should therefore report validity and faithfulness separately and pair verifier-driven repair with semantic auditing.

sections.title: B AGENT IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Figure 3 summarizes the agent loop and its tools. The orchestrator alternates between reasoning and tool use. run ends when the Lean REPL first reports pass, when the orchestrator declares success (refused while its latest REPL check has failed), or after 24 steps. The prompt also asks the orchestrator to check faithfulness before finishing, but the runner does not enforce this; semantic judging is applied only to the final statement. 15 Figure 3: Agent orchestration logic. The orchestrator calls optional drafting, search, and compiler-feedback tools in Lean 4. Figure 4: Our agent (config 111) with three orchestrators. All three converge to 5865% accepted outputs despite different one-shot baselines (2033%; Appendix J.5). B.1 PROMPT ASSEMBLY The system prompt is constructed from three modular components: (i) task definition establishing the core translation objective, (ii) general usage guide containing fixed best practices for Lean 4 code generation, and (iii) capability block that is dynamically populated based on the factorial configuration (T, F, S). This structure holds the agents semantic goal and coding standards (i and ii) fixed, while selectively enabling or disabling external tools (iii) to isolate the effect of each capability. We assemble (i) and (ii) into Shared Base Prompt, shown below, while the capability block definitions are provided in Appendix B.3. B.2 SHARED BASE PROMPT

sections.title: Base System Prompt
sections.content: You are an expert Lean4 translation agent. Your task is to translate natural-language mathematical statement into faithful Lean4 syntax (NOT proof). The final result must: - import Mathlib at the very top - compile in Mathlib - be semantically faithful to the original statement - end with := by sorry You are NOT proving anything. You are only producing correctly typed, correct-meaning Lean statement. GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS FOR CODE GENERATION The Lean file MUST start with: import Mathlib The Lean file MUST contain exactly ONE final translated statement representing the original natural-language meaning. The final statement MUST end with: := by sorry Do NOT write any proof code before := by sorry (no by, simp, have, calc, etc. anywhere before the final := by sorry). Do NOT invent new definitions, axioms, constants, or placeholder structures. Prefer robust formulations: use quantifiers, membership, and characterizations rather than fragile definitional equalities. 16 Only finish when the last written version: (1) compiles in Mathlib (if lean4_repl_runner is available) (2) is semantically faithful to the original statement When both are satisfied, return: "status": "success" B.3 TOOL-AVAILABILITY BLOCKS Each factorial configuration (T, F, S) determines which tools are exposed to the agent. We implement this by modular prompt template in which the AVAILABLE TOOLS block is constructed by including the corresponding tool-specification entries and omitting inactive ones. sections.content: Outputs. The validation set has every compiling output that GPT-5.2 rejects (grade below 9, the rule of Section 4.3 and Figure 2) and that has human-majority label: 64 outputs of our agent (Batch A) and 5 of Aristotle (Batch B), 69 in all, on 66 statements; the human majority judges 57 of them unfaithful. The one-shot set has every compiling output of the seven one-shot systems that GPT-5.2 rejects, on statements whose recorded input matches the benchmark: 142 outputs on 105 statements. For Table 8, which uses the criterion of Figure 1, we also reviewed the three compiling outputs that only Gemini-2.5-Pro rejects (Goedel-Prover on BC007, one-shot GPT-5.2 on BC129 and BC130); their first stage also saw Geminis grade and reason, and all three are translation errors. The validation results are in Tables 6 and 7 (Section 4.1). Procedure. Both sets use the instructions of our first review run, on the later models (Section 4.3; Appendix H), with three changes. The first stage names the systems under review. It may read only its input file, the textbook sources, and its own Lean checks, so that the human labels, which are stored elsewhere on the same machine, stay hidden; in the validation run, the agents logs show that no other file was opened. It sees only rejected outputs, so there is no accepted output of another model to compare with. The stages run in order: Claude Opus 5.5 agents in Claude Code with the Lean REPL review batches of 12 statements; GPT-6.1 Sol reviews each output with the first review in view; and GPT-6.1 Sol decides the outputs on which exactly one review finds translation error. Both stages see the statement, its source excerpt, the output, and the grades and stated reasons of GPT-5.2 and of Claude Sonnet 5, as for the later models; for Aristotle and the one-shot systems we obtained the Sonnet 5 grades with the papers judge prompt. For the three outputs that only Gemini-2.5-Pro rejects, the first stage also sees Geminis grade and reason. No stage sees human label. Final classes follow the rule of the later-model review, which reproduces its released classes exactly. The prompts, both reviews, the discussion, and the reviewers Lean checks are released. Details. Over all 69 outputs, the review agrees with the human majority on 79.7% (κ = 0.41); pairs of reviewers agree on 69.674.6% (κ = 0.120.27). Of the four outputs that the review flags and the majority accepts, two are Lean-verified errors: A-008 (BC148) omits b, and its statement is false for < a; A-094 (BC019) asks for an isomorphism with the multiplicative monoid of ZMod (2p), which no group has, so it is false for cyclic groups. A-027 (BC160) replaces Riemann with Lebesgue integrability, and A-012 (BC072) admits an extra case with Nat.card = 0. H.3 SECOND JUDGE AND RE-GRADING Requiring Sonnet 5 to reject as well keeps all four translation errors and 29 of the other 49 graded rejections, so the share of real errors rises from 7% to 12%. With five more GPT-5.2 calls per rejected output, 37 of the 50 rejections that are not translation errors stay rejected, majority accepts 2 of the 4 errors, and 4 of 40 sampled accepted outputs flip to rejection. H.4 CHECKS IN LEAN Part of this can be checked without trusting any reviewer. Lean-checked certificates cover 15 of the rejected outputs; the three kinds of evidence overlap and show different things. For 9 of the 10 pairs in which GPT-5.2 accepts one models output and rejects the others  (Table 28)  , Lean proves the two statements equivalent, by definitional unfolding or direct correspondence of their hypotheses and conclusions, yet GPT-5.2 grades them differently; one pair is textually identical and graded 10 and 2. For 4 of the 9 rejections with wrong stated reason, Lean refutes that reason, which does not by itself show the rest of the output faithful. For 4 rejected outputs, Lean proves equivalence to an output that human reviewers accepted for the same statement. All 15 are among the outputs that the review classifies as not translation errors. 31 Claude Opus 5.5 agents wrote the Lean proofs; fixed checker decides whether they count. checked equivalence shows that two statements have the same truth conditions; it supports, but does not by itself establish, that they make the same claim as the natural-language statement. The checker places each output verbatim, without its import line, in its own namespace (R for the rejected output, for the other models accepted output or for the human-accepted output), so the agents cannot change the statements. For an equivalence, the certificate must have type R-statement P-statement up to universe instantiation and definitional unfolding, both directions must be functions that use their hypothesis, and #print axioms must show no sorryAx and nothing beyond propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. For stated reason, every recorded claim must compile under the same axiom check. Table 30 summarizes the outcomes; the release contains every proof and check record. BC046 could not be run through the checker. H.5 SUPPLYING DEFINITIONS TO THE JUDGE Giving the judge fixed block of library definitions does not change its rejections of outputs that humans judge faithful. GPT-5.2 received the Mathlib definitions that each output uses, extracted from the Lean environment by fixed rule and capped in length, with the prompt otherwise unchanged. On the 74 human-labeled rejections of our agent and Aristotle, with three calls per output and condition, the judge accepts by majority the same 8 of the 16 human-faithful outputs with and without the block, and 1 and 0 of the 58 human-unfaithful ones. On the later models, acceptance of the 32 outputs that the review classes as judge errors goes from 10 to 11, with five outputs changing in either direction. For each output, metaprogram elaborates the code on top of Mathlib and collects the constants used by the types of its declarations and by the values of its definitions. We keep constants from Mathlib modules only (core constants such as Eq, Nat, or HMul.hMul are dropped), in order of first use and at most 30, and give each its signature, its docstring, and, for definition, its value when short; the block is capped at 6000 characters, limit reached for 41 of the 128 outputs. The judge receives the papers system prompt and user message unchanged, with this block added after the Lean code. Each output is graded three times under each condition and counts as accepted if at least two grades are 9 or more; for the later models, the condition without definitions uses the first three re-grading calls of Appendix H.3. H.6 DEFECTIVE STATEMENTS Of the 11 rejections on defective statements  (Table 28)  , four concern statements that are false as written, as in their sources, and here the two later models differ. Opus adds the hypotheses that make three of them true: nonempty factors for the compactness of (BC179, BC180) and Hausdorff for the one-point compactification (BC218). GPT-5.2 rejects these repairs and gives GPT-6 Astras literal translations 10. On the fourth (BC092; Table 32 lists all flagged statements), it does the opposite, rejecting Astras literal statement and accepting Opuss repair. Our review counts both the literal translation and the minimal repair as not translation errors; GPT-5.2 follows neither policy consistently. Without the 18 flagged statements, GPT-5.2 reports gaps of 7.2 and 9.6 points for GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5, and the review classifies 1 of 15 and 3 of 20 of their rejections as translation errors; for our agent, humans confirm 45 of its 55 rejections (Appendix I).
